name: Contrast in Photography: Choose What Deserves Attention
description: Learn how contrast in photography uses tone, colour, texture and ideas to guide attention, preserve atmosphere and support deliberate composition choices.

step.name: Decide how much contrast the photograph needs
step.text: Contrast in photography describes differences between tones, colours, textures or ideas. Those differences can separate elements, reveal a relationship or influence where attention falls. Notice the contrast already present before trying to increase it. A subtle distinction in mist or a quiet colour relationship may be precisely what attracted you. Stronger contrast is useful when it supports that response. Restraint can mean leaving an adjustment unused, reducing a competing highlight or preserving a gentle transition. step.name: Watch the relationships
step.text: Watch where light falls, what remains in shadow and how those areas change. Direction, diffusion and reflected light affect the relationships you can photograph. Moving your viewpoint may change the background behind an element as much as the light on it.

step.name: Choose what you need to retain
step.text: Protect highlight detail when that detail matters. A bright reflection or deep silhouette may serve a different purpose. Check the result and choose exposure for the information and feeling you want to retain.

step.name: Look beyond the overall tonal range
step.text: Tonal contrast concerns differences in brightness. The same patch can appear lighter or darker depending on its surroundings. Look at adjacent areas as well as the overall range of the image.

step.name: Choose the separation that serves the photograph
step.text: Strong separation may help a shape stand out, while a subtle transition can preserve atmosphere. There is no requirement to place the greatest contrast on one named subject: several areas may form the relationship you want to show.

step.name: Consider visual weight
step.text: Notice how much of the frame each colour occupies and how it relates to nearby tones. A small bright area may attract more attention than a large subdued one.

step.name: Use HDR when the scene needs it
step.text: Merging bracketed exposures can retain detail across a scene whose brightness range exceeds what one exposure records adequately. Movement between exposures may cause merging problems. The final rendering can be subtle or pronounced. Use the additional information only when it supports the photograph. Restraint question: Does the image need detail throughout the tonal range, or are its highlights and shadows already doing useful work? Editing practice · Compare first

step.name: Choose an editing tool for a specific purpose
step.text: Curves Adjust tonal relationships or separation. Check that highlights, shadows and gentle transitions you value remain intact. Texture and Clarity Change local midtone detail. Apply them selectively when surface character matters and watch for halos or an unnatural appearance. Colour grading Explore relationships between highlights, midtones and shadows. Keep the change only when the colour supports the intended atmosphere. Dodge and burn Lighten or darken specific areas to adjust attention and visual weight.
